name: membrane
intent: Wrap every capability that crosses a subsystem boundary - arguments passed in and objects, callbacks or results handed back out - so a restriction on the interface applies transitively instead of guarding only the first reference, and the whole wrapped set can be revoked at once.
problem: An interface hands out a reference that carries a restriction - a read-only view, a tenant-scoped directory, a sandboxed plugin API - but the objects exchanged through it stay raw: a callee that returns a capability to itself, or stores a capability the caller passed in, gives one side an unguarded route around the restriction. Guarding only the initial reference (an attenuated or revocable forwarder) therefore fails exactly when the far side cannot be trusted to respect the attenuation.
context: Object-capability settings where references are the only route to authority: plugin and extension hosts, multi-tenant object graphs, in-process confinement of foreign code (agents, macro languages, browser-style sandboxes), capability filesystems, and any boundary whose policy must hold over everything reachable from a reference. Applicable when the host can intercept every call through a reference and keep a per-membrane identity map; where references can be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper, or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
benefits: The restriction is transitive: objects returned from calls, callbacks passed in, iterators and nested graphs are wrapped too, so the policy cannot be side-stepped by exchanging references.
Both directions are covered symmetrically: the untrusted side never receives a raw reference to the outer side, and the outer side never receives a raw reference into the protected graph.
One revocation point: killing the membrane invalidates every reference ever handed out through it, which is how whole-subsystem authority is withdrawn in capability systems.
The policy lives in the wrapper, not in the protected objects: the subsystem stays unaware that it is mediated, and clients need no cooperation to be contained.
An identity map keeps the wrapper world coherent: a given object always yields the same wrapper, so equality, caches, memoisation and revocation by reference keep working inside one membrane.
tradeoffs: Identity and typing change at the boundary: the wrapper is a different object, so identity tests, type checks, serialisation and pattern matching see the wrapper unless the identity map and the host's semantics are handled deliberately.

Completeness is the load-bearing invariant and it decays silently - every newly added method, callback, exception path or marshalling route that hands out a raw reference is an escape the membrane cannot detect.

Check-then-forward races under concurrency: when the enable/revocation state is read and the call forwarded as separate steps, a request can slip through after revocation (the TOCTTOU flaw found in the revocable membrane, and the analogous revocation race found in capability operating systems).
Cost per crossing: an extra interposed call (two on a round trip) plus identity-map lookups, and a wrapper object plus map entry for every wrapped referent unless weak references are used.
Revocation is all-or-nothing per membrane; per-reference revocation needs a revocable forwarder inside it, and nested membranes multiply wrappers and map bookkeeping.
Debugging, stack traces, logging and introspection see wrappers rather than domain objects, and a wrapper that forwards everything hides the API it mediates.

participants.responsibility: Interposes on every invocation crossing the boundary, applies the membrane's policy (attenuation, mediation, revocation) and remains the only route between the two sides.
The per-object stand-in handed across the boundary: it forwards calls to the wrapped object and wraps whatever it returns, so the policy travels with the reference.
Calls only through the membrane and never holds a raw reference to the inner side; anything it receives has already been wrapped.
The objects behind the boundary whose authority is reduced; they receive wrapped arguments and must reach the outer side through the membrane as well.
Per-membrane registry mapping each wrapped object to its one wrapper (and back), so identity and equality stay stable and wrappers are never duplicated; entries are held weakly.
Optional companion object, handed only to the principal that must retain control, which turns the whole membrane off at once instead of revoking reference by reference.

use_cases: Plugin and extension hosts that must let foreign code use the objects it was given without letting it reach anything beyond them (sandboxed browser objects, editor extensions, in-process agents).

Multi-tenant object graphs where a tenant-scoped directory or session object is handed to another component and every file, directory or handle it returns must inherit the same restriction - the transitive read-only property that Tahoe-LAFS wanted and could not enforce because its model does not separate data from capabilities.
Read-only or quota-limited views where the callee cannot be trusted to respect an attenuated capability, so a returned raw capability would restore full authority.
Shutting a subsystem down: giving a component a set of references that must all die together at plugin unload, session end or workflow cancellation.
In-process confinement of foreign code (formula and macro languages, pluggable rule engines, untrusted extensions) where a full process or VM boundary is too heavy.
Capability filesystems and object stores whose returned handles or URLs must be re-wrapped so the policy travels with the data rather than with the first lookup.

Agoric Endo SES Compartments and lockdown use separate globals plus explicitly endowed authorities to confine third-party JavaScript; a membrane is the right companion when those endowments or returned objects must be mediated transitively rather than copied raw.

Google Caja's ES5/3 taming layer uses tamed/feral twins and wraps arguments and return values across its gadget boundary, a concrete membrane-style integration for legacy embedded HTML, CSS and JavaScript (now archived, so do not treat it as a maintained security baseline).

Salesforce's near-membrane library places a JavaScript membrane between realms and wraps non-primitive crossing values in proxies to preserve object-graph integrity; it is a useful implementation reference when integrity mediation, rather than process isolation, is the requirement.
avoid_when: Only the initial reference needs guarding and the far side can be trusted to respect attenuation: an attenuating (read-only) forwarder is enough, and a revocable forwarder covers single-reference revocation.
The untrusted code should not share the process at all: a sandbox (separate process, VM, seccomp, WebAssembly) is a stronger and simpler boundary than an in-process membrane.

The runtime cannot intercept calls through a reference, or references can be forged, dereferenced or reached by reflection/marshalling: build the boundary in a runtime with unforgeable references instead of adopting a membrane that any raw pointer can bypass.
The wrapped unit is a single short-lived call: the wrapper and identity-map machinery costs more than the boundary it protects.
The requirement is observation rather than restriction (logging, metrics, tracing): a decorator or proxy that forwards without wrapping both directions is simpler and does not distort identity.
anti_patterns: Guarding only the first reference and calling it a membrane: the callee returns a raw capability to itself (or stores the caller's raw argument) and the restriction is gone - an attenuating forwarder is not a membrane.
Wrapping without an identity map, so the same object returns a fresh wrapper each time and equality, caches and revocation-by-reference all break while the registry grows without bound.
Wrapping only outbound results but not inbound arguments (or the reverse), leaving whichever side holds the raw reference able to reach around the policy.
Revoking by dropping references while calls are in flight, or checking an enable flag and forwarding later: an in-flight or racing call still crosses after revocation.
Presenting an in-process membrane as a security boundary in a runtime where reflection, FFI, serialisation or raw pointers can obtain the unwrapped object.
design_principles: Complete mediation: every access crosses the membrane; a single bypass path voids the policy for the whole graph.
Least privilege / transitive attenuation: the authority handed across the boundary must shrink together with everything reachable from it.
Information hiding: the raw reference stays on its own side; only the wrapper travels.
Single point of revocation: revoke the membrane, not each reference, so authority cannot be forgotten in one place.
Symmetry: verify both directions of the boundary (arguments inward, results and callbacks outward), because either one is sufficient to escape.
best_practices: Wrap on every crossing, in both directions: arguments before forwarding in, and results, callbacks, iterators and error payloads before handing back out.
Keep exactly one wrapper per (membrane, object) in a weak identity map so identity is stable and the map never retains the wrapped graph.
Make the policy explicit per membrane (allowed operations, attenuation, revocation) and keep it in the wrapper rather than scattered through the protected objects.
Keep the revocation check and the forward atomic, or fold the state into the forwarding step (the repair used in the cited analyses), so in-flight calls cannot slip through.
Revoke the membrane as a whole and hand the revoker only to the principal that must keep control; do not hand out per-reference kill switches unless the design needs them.
Test with a hostile, maximal-behaviour client: try to obtain a direct reference through returns, callbacks, exceptions and nested objects, and assert that every crossing was mediated.
Treat the membrane as a complement to process or VM isolation, not a replacement, wherever the runtime lets raw references escape.
sources: Deian Stefan & John C. Mitchell, Analysing Object-Capability Patterns With Murϕ (2011), sections 2.2.2 (attenuated and membrane forwarders) and 4.1.2 (the revocable membrane's TOCTTOU violation) - the catalog's cited source for the Membrane row.

Toby Murray, Analysing Object-Capability Security (FCS-ARSPA-WITS 2008), section 2 (the membrane running example) and section 3.1 (the revocable membrane) - the formal account of the transitive property the pattern must uphold.

Mark S. Miller, Robust Composition: Towards a Unified Approach to Access Control and Concurrency Control (PhD thesis, Johns Hopkins University, 2006) - origin of the membrane forwarder in the object-capability literature.
